fileDesc.titleStmt: LETTERS OF HUMPHREY PRIDEAUX SOMETIME DEAN OF NORWICH TO JOHN ELLIS SOMETIME UNDER-SECRETARY OF STATE 1674-1722. ED. BY EDWARD MAUND THOMPSON. CAMDEN SOCIETY NEW SERIES XV. 1875.

text.p: Oxford , Sept 20th, 1681.

I had sooner written to you since my return, had I found any thing here worth informeing you. Yesterday was the election of our mayor, and the man choosen is one Alderman Bailey, whom they put up out of his order to be mayor that they might put by Mr. Harris, the only person in the corporation that is for the Kings interest; but this being an unpardonable crime among our Whiggish townsmen, they have set up this old blade, although more then half doted, because somewhat more agreeable to their principles. The old Lady Lovelace is very busy at all businesses in the town to influence them her way, and she is now grown so zealous a Whig that she goes every Sunday to the Lady Angleseys to make one of the holy sisters at her conventicle. By her and some other that come hither our Oxonians are made so courageous
that they talk nothing now but of wageing war with ye King, and the resolution is concluded on that Westminster Hall must decide it between the King and them concerneing the town clerk. However, they thought fit first to give his Majesty some warneing, and therefore some of them attended with a petition at Newmarket for Princes admission, but could find no one there that would introduce them to ye King, so that they were forced to wait till the King came forth to walk, and then they delivered it to him in the fields, and he ordered them to attend the Lt. Conway for an answer, which was a very severe reprofe for their ill carriage to his Majesty both in this and many other affairs; which made them so angry, that when they came home they talked of nothing but of admitteing Prince forthwith and defying the King. For they say the charter which obliged them to have the Kings approbation of their town clerk was given them since the Kings return, and if they forfeit that they tell us they are not concerned, they having other charters whereby they hold all their other privileges in more ample manner and without any such reserve. But when the time came they only admitted Prince as deputy, to serve in time of vacancy; but its supposed they will never otherwise supply ye vacancy, thinking by the trick to evade the Kings prerogative. The only man in the town of any note that is true to the Kings interest is Mr Harris, who is a very honest and very understandeing man, and, although son-in-law to Alderman Wright, yet acts so contrary to him that ye alderman is become a violent and irreconcilable enemy to him, and by his contrivance it is that he is put by from being mayor this year. He is one of the most sufficient men among them, being worth above ten thousand pounds. He is a very fit man to be town clerk, having been bred a lawyer, but he is not willing to take ye trouble. Sr Thomas Chamberlain, one of ye Deputy-Lieutenants of this county, now lies at the point of death; he will leave 2 daughters behind him, each of which will be
worth 15000l apiece. I shall take care that Mr Guise wait on you before he leave England; he goes from hence on Wednesday; by him you shall again hear from me.

Our townsmen still continue in the same humour of disputing the Kings prerogative with him. Princes speech was made at the election of ye new mayor. If you can remember our Town Hall, there is a large yard before it, and there the rabble meet while the wiser heads of them, which they call the Common Council, are consulteing within whom they shall bring out to them; for the Common Council choose two and bring them out into a balkony looking into the yard wherein the rabble meet, and of them two he which they choose is mayor of the town. After Bailey had been thus brought and choosen mayor, then Prince came forth and began, "Gentlemen, I have something to say to you. You have choosen me town clerk and I will defend your right," and so proceeded to brag what he would doe against the King (not without some rude reflections) in defence of the town privileges, and then
told them how ill they were used at Newmarket, and at last (as his very words were) he told them indeed he thought the King of himself a very honest man, but he was drawn away by evil councillors; and then Necessity Holloway, being pro-Recorder, stopped him from proceedeing any farther, not that he misliked the matter of his speech, but, as he himself told me, because he thought it not so proper that he should speak so much in his own business. The way they are resolved to proceed they tell me is this. Prince is to sue the mayor for admission in the Kings Bench, and then they say an order must of course issue out to cause the mayor to give a reason why he doth not admit him, and then ye mayor will give the Kings refusal of approbation as the reason, and crave the judgement of ye Court upon it; and they say they have it under the hands of the best lawyers in England that the Court must declare in favour of them, for the charter wherein the King hath this prerogative of approveing ye recorder and town clerk reserved to him was granted by this King since his return; and they make count to cancel this charter and stand to that they had before. However, it seems their courage doth somewhat cool, for yesterday they went in a full body to the Earl of Angleseys to crave his assistance in the case; but I suppose all assistance will come to late in behalf of Prince after so seditious a speech. It seems Alderman Wright is turned out of ye Commission of the Peace for the town, as well as for the county, on the account of the story I writ you of in my last. It seems our plenipotentiaries yt went to Newmarket were likewise very coursely treated at Cambridge; for the innkeeper where they lodged swinged them in their reckoneing most abominably, making them pay five times the price for every thing they had; and hireing a chamber there to lay some of their things till their return, which was but 3 days, they
made them pay 20s for it, and, when expostulated with, told them it was accordeing to the rate gentlemen paid at Oxford when ye Parliament was here, and therefore they had no reason to complain; and when they scrupled payment they were in danger of being had before the mayor, but to avoid this they were contented to pay what was demanded; but all put together, and Tompsons narrative of their journey in the last Intelligence, is such a heavy grievance unto them that their great hearts can scarce bear up under the affliction of it. I hope this will put them upon such resentments as to make ym loose their charter. Dr Hammond is married and Jack Benson is towards it, being got into as bad an entanglement of love as his brother Sam was. I have nothing more.

TEI.text:
Oxford , Thursday, Sept. 29, 1681.
In my last I promised you an account of ye Earl of Angleseys reception. Accordeing to ye appointment, he was conducted into the town last Tuesday by the townsmen in great state, and he and his two sons made freemen of the town. He made a speech to them, wherein he took notice of their disagreeing with the University, and offered his service to reconcile them to us, or doe them any other kindness that lay in his power. It seems they promised him, when they first went to him, that if he would stand their friend at Court, now the Duke of Buckingham their steward hath no access there, they would have a burgesses place always at his service for whomsoever he should recommend; and this it was that made his Ldship so readily comply with them; and now
they begin to defy the Lt. Norris, they having gotten as they think so potent a protection against him; but I suppose his Ldship will not think fit to interfere with any one for their sakes. After he was sworn, a dinner was made ready for him at the mayors, where he was splendidly entertained. The townsmen have had a Common Council to consider of ye affront put upon them in Tompsons Intelligence, and have voted it as a scandalous libel against their most honourable Corporation, and an action is ordered to be entered against him next term. But Tompson is not the only man yt makes sport with their voyage to Newmarket. Alderman Wright lately going before Brazen Nose Coll. a fresh man came out, and spying him past by called after him "Run, Alderman, run; the Black guard are coming!" which put the alderman into so violent a passion that he was scarce himself all that day after. Whenever he comes, he speaks scurrulously of the King. It seems, when ye alderman was at Newmarket with his petition, the King walking in ye fields met Nel Gwyn, and Nel called to him, "Charles, I hope I shall have your company at night, shall I not?" With this story the Alderman makes a great deal of work wherever he comes. He says he had often heard bad things of the King, but now his own eyes have seen it. They are mighty at consultation concerneing ye management of their law suit, and doubt mightily how it will be managed against them, whither the Attorney General will plead against the granteing Prince a mandamus , or let that be granted and after proceed against them with a quo warranto . But which way soever it be, they make mighty sure of their cause; and all the rabble of ye town are for living and dying by it. Dr Morton came hither on Tuesday, and on Friday goes for Ireland.

text.p:
Nothing happened worth informeing you at our sessions, but only that 2 malefactors were condemned to death (one for killing her bastard and a rogue for cutteing a purse), and the pro-Town Clerk officiated not in his place. It seems ye townsmen doe not keep to their first courage, but begin to be cautious and wary how they give offence, and therefore have thought fit not to let Prince officiate in the place as they first designed, but have appointed another to doe it. The Vice-Chancellor and ye Bp. have had a great consult about the Secretaries letter concerneing ye reneweing our commission, and have agreed to put in Dr Parrot, Dr Levied, Dr Jane, Dr Beson, Warden of New College, Dr Lloyd, and I think Mr Guise. The Bp. is very desirous he should be in, but the Vice-Chancellor made an exception that he was not so proper as being only a Mr of Arts; but when I went to him and told him he was not to be looked on as an ordinary Mr of Arts, but as a gentleman which lives in town upon his estate which is worth 500l
per annum, and therefore sufficient to qualify him for such an office in any county in England, he seemed to be as willing as the Bp., but whither they will return his name or no I can not tell. I desire yt you would give me advice from ye Secretaries, where you will certainly know; for, if his name be not put in at ye Secretaries, I will attempt to doe it at the Lord Chancellors, and I hope there I shall not fail; but if that trouble were saved I should be glad, and therefore I beg your assistance in it. I wonder ye Secretary should say he doth not know him. He knew him once to doe him a very great unkindness in making the Archbp. his enemy, although he did not design it. He is a gentleman of as great worth and eminence in that way of learneing he hath addicted himself to as any in England, or, I believe, in any other country in Europe, and on that account is an ornament to the University, and will er long appear so to the whole nation. He is an extraordinary person and I cannot say enough of him, and beside him I believe you will find few of his estate to devote themselves so industriously to their studies, or of his parts to make so good progress in them. And beside, his good inclinations to the Church doth sufficiently appear in that, in his circumstances and in so ill times, he would go into orders to be rendered thereby ye more capable of serving it. I think such a man is not to be affronted, and now his name hath been mentioned on this occasion it would be an affront not to be put in. Pray use your interest to effect it, and if that doth not succeed I will use mine with the Chancellor. He is married and lives here in the town, and therefore considereing all his qualifications I know not who can be fitter. The Secretary having himself mentioned Dr Jane, the Bp. thought not fit to put in either Dr Hammond or Dr Smith, to avoid envy to our college. Sr William Walter already begins to make an interest to be knight of the shire next Parliament, and will I suppose without any great difficulty carry it, he being a person of general good esteem in ye county. Tomorrow I go to the funeral of
Sr Thomas Chamberlain, where I suppose I shall meet most of the gentry of ye county, and perchance shall be able to inform you of something worth observation from thence. St Cyprian is now finished, as likewise a book of Dugdales of Heraldry; it contains ye first principles of it, and the catalogue of ye Nobility and Baronets of ye 3 kingdoms.
Oxford , Feb. 23, 1682 .

I have yours of Tuesday, and know not what to say to your affair. It is better have the employment you mention then have none at all, especially if you are sent so honourably to it as by the King himself and have his promise of a provision, but to be always mereteing and receive no reward is an hard case. This employment is not worth medleing with, in my judgment, without a future prospect of advantage; if you have any such, it is better embark in it then lie idle, but were it my case I would make my market as good as I could and would not ask less then to be Clerk of ye Council, and old Brown will er long make a place vacant there; you can best judge of it. My good wishes I can put it, but my judgment in cases of this nature is not to be relied on, because not versed in ye affairs of Court or acquainted how your circumstances stand there; only this, I would always lay down as a general rule, to accept of that which is beneath a mans expectations rather then have nothing at all. Your chief point will be to secure a friend which will solicit for you in your absence in case an opportunity happen, and next to take care, while in France, yt the faults of the inexperienced ambassador doe not lie at
your door, for I perceive, in effect, you are to be sent his governor, and often it happens to such yt they bear the blame for their pupils fault, whither they can help them or no. I wish you all the success you can desire or expect in this affair, and the best prosperity in all other.

P.S. If it give you not too much trouble, I would desire you to remember your promise of buying me a beaver, such as is proper for a divine, provided not too big; and get it put into a box and sent to the Oxford carriers either at ye Saracens Head in Snow Hill or ye Oxford Arms in Warwic Lane, which ye person of whom you buy it of I suppose will take care. If it be not sent away as soon as bought, there will be danger of a change afterword.
Oxford, 12 March, 1682 .

Our assizes are ended without affordeing me anything observable to inform you of. Here was very little business on ye Crown side. Only a poor fellow is condemned to be hanged for breaking prison. He was last Michaelmas condemned at ye town sessions for cutteing a purse, that having it seems been long his trade, for it appeared by his hand he was formerly burnt for it. However, intercession having been made to the King for him, he was repreved in order to transportation; but before orders came concerneing it he broke prison, and, being a while after caught again at his old trade and put into Newgate, our gaylor challenged him as his, and being brought hither hath sentence of death passed upon him again for breaking his prison; and now I suppose, without any further hopes of mercy, he is to prepare for hangeing, he being a most notorious
rogue, as it sufficiently appeared at his trial. That which was most observable was a most terrible abhorrence of ye association presented to the bench by the grand jury, and the Lt. Norris being present undertook ye presenteing of it. It is worded at the highest pitch of loyalty and zeal, and in the end of it they promise ye King yt, whenever he shall think fit to call another Parliament, they will choose only such as shall be acceptable to the King, and will be for the preserving the succession of the Crown to the right heir. Levinz sat judge for ye Crown, and Atkings in ye other court. Friday morneing was wholly taken up in giving ye charge, which was very long, and therefore he made this excuse for it, that there being very little business he had nothing else to entertain ye company with. In his charge he insisted against prosecuteing Protestant dissenters on ye Act of 35th of Queen Elizabeth, and urged some arguments to prove that it was not designed it should be put in execution against them, particularly that of inflicteing lesser penalties since, which he looked on as disalloweing of those rigorous ones to be inflicted by that Act, and told us that it was never but once put in execution, and that was against some of Colchester; which part of his charge gave us here some offence. Aaron Smiths business is put of till the next assize, some punctilio in law being wonteing for bringeing him to his trial this assizes. We had great expectations of a trial at the other court between ye Lt. Norris and Brom Whorwood, about their quarrel in the Town Hall at the election of ye Town Clerk. Broom brought an action of battery against my Lt. for beateing him, and my Lt. an action of scandalum magnatum against Broom for calleing him young fool. But the Bp. of
Oxford interposeing spoiled the sport and made up the matter between them; for in truth ye Lt. Norris first began the quarrel, and called Brom old fool before he called him young fool; and beside it was reather hypothetically then categorically said, for my Lt. calleing him old fool, he replied, "If I am an old fool you are a young fool," and therefore I think his Lordship did very wisely to submit it to the Bps. arbitration. Whenever there is a Parliament its certain this old knave will never more be choosen here, by reason of the trick he hath put upon his brother representative; for Alderman Wright taking care of dischargeing the alehouse and paying the bills of their canvas, when he came to Whorwood to be reimbursed his share of it, the old knave told him if he had payed the bills already there was no need for him to concern himself any further, and ye Alderman could not get as much as a fartheing of him for bearing the expenses of three elections for him; and on this account he is out of all expectations here for ye future, and therefore puts in very violently for an interest at Abington. The town are mightily affrighted with the expectation of a quo warranto , for they having reprieved a wench condemned here for killing her bastard 4 months without the Kings autority to warrant their doing of it, they all give their charter for gon if the King should come upon them for the forfeiture. And that they should receive any favour herein is what, considereing their carriage to the King, is what they cannot reasonably expect; and I hope his Majesty will think so too. Dr Elliot, an eminent physician of this place, is lately dead. The Earl of Northampton next week takes his leave of the University and goes to travel. I thank you for ye trouble you are pleased to give your self in buying me an hat, but ye carrier hath not as yet brought him hither.
P.S. Pray lets know what is like to become of the charter of London, and with use is made of the information I gave concerneing Norwich.
Oxford, Aug. 6, 1684.

I have ye favour of two of yours to acknowledge. Both of them came to my hands at Woodstock, but now I am again at Oxford. Our Act ended here with ye expulsion of both ye Terrefilii , but that hath not put an end to ye bustle which we are now in on two accounts ; ye one is ye concern of ye whole University, ye other of a private college. Ye University concern is about ye town carter. It seems, to induce them to surrender it, ye Earl of Abington promised them ye addition of several new grants, and in order thereto a petition was presented to ye King in council concerneing it, which contained 5 points; but, ye University apprehendeing that ye King by granteing it would prejudice us, they presented a counter petition in answer to it, and upon a full hearing in council ye town petition was rejected in every point. This was about 5 months since. But ye Lord Abington, not acquiesceing in it, hath ever since been employing his interest in ye town behalf to doe us all ye prejudice he can, and acts very vehemently and peevishly in the thing, and so ye business now stands; but we do not doubt our interest herein, and I hope er long I shall be able to give you an account of our good success. The other affair is concerneing Magd. Coll. Ye divinity lecturer being dead, ye college proceeded to an election, and by a great majority choose on Dr Bailey into ye place, at which Dr Smith, formerly Sr Joseph Williamsons chaplain, being ye senr, thinks himself aggrieved, because at ye colleges petition ye Bishop of Winchester made an injunction yt all offices and lectures should be disposed of accordeing
to seniority, supposeing ye persons capable. Upon this ye Dr makes his appeal to ye Bishop, and upon a full hearing ye Bp. determines in favour of Smith, and orders ye college to proceed to a new election and make choice of Smith. Ye college refuses to submit to this sentence; hereupon ye 9 seniors are put out of commons; hereupon ye college address to ye D. of Ormond, and by him present a petition to ye King for redress; and ye Bp. hath been served with an order to proceed no further herein, the King having appointed to have ye hearing of it himself, and there it now rests. In ye meantime Dr Smiths party, which are only two, have presented a libel of accusation to ye Bishop against their head. The crimes they accuse him of are chiefly corruption in soloing of places, and knavery in falsifying ye college register in a thing that was entered there by order of King and council on ye decision of a former controversy in Dr Pierces time heard before ye council, while I suppose you were of ye University, which being much to the infamy of Dr Pierce, when he sold his headship to the present man, it seems one part of ye bargain was that he should race all this out of ye register, as he should have an opportunity of so doing; and accordingly, to make good his promise, this honest man, finding ye whole to be contained within two pages, pasts them both together and so made ye whole disappear. They are now at Farnham about it, but what ye result will be I know not. What we have now don at ye press ye Gazette hath er this told you. Dr Brady hath lately published altogether several tracts he formerly published against some antimonarchical antiquaries, and in ye preface promises us ye 1st part of his long talked of History of England to be published in Michaelmas term. He hath been long a searcher
after English antiquity and pretends to have made great discoveries. What they are we shall know when his book comes forth. There is a book lately published by some of ye foreign seminaries against ye Bp. of Winchester in answer to his lately put forth against ye papists, in which the old man is dealt very rudely with. Drayden hath published a translation of Maimburgs History of ye League, as he tells us at ye Kings command. Judge Windham being dead, its talked Roger North, ye Keepers brother, will succeed him. But for such sort of news I refer you to ye news papers you have public with you. My house will be coverd by Michaelmas, and when it is habitable I shall fix my residence in it to ye end of my days. I wish you good health and all things that can be good in that country.
Oxford, July 9th, 1685.

I have received yours, and accordeing to your order have paid your brother 5l. Your former making me hope I should speedily see you here made me defer writing, least my letter might come too late to find you in Dublin. Our rebellion is now over, Monmouth and all his party being routed. Instead thereof we have now got a standeing army, a thing the nation hath long been
jealous of; but I hope ye King will no otherwise use it then to secure our peace. The war now from ye field I suppose will pass into ye roads, which we must expect will a while be infested with the remainder of those rogues. You will have a more exact account of these transactions from London then I am able to give you from this place. Our good Bp. is fallen very ill, and I fear will not long last. We begin already to be solicitous who may be his successor. I believe it may be your tutor, and I am of an opinion he may not be so unfit a man as some apprehend. The Bp. of Chichester is lately dead and ye sea of Peterborough is vacant by ye translation of Bp. Lloyd to Norwich. Trelawny will be a Bishop somewhere before all those vacancies be supplied, its supposed at Bristol, the Bp. of that place being to be translated to Peterborough. We have no Act this year, although ye greatest number of Doctors that I ever knew in all faculties, especially in divinity. The rebellion hath been ye occasion of this intermission. Dr Stillingfleet hath lately published a book worth your seeing, containeing an historical account of ye British Church before its suppression by ye Saxon invasion. I shall doe your brother all the service I can, but I believe my time in the college will now be short, especially if ye Bp. dyes. I have now been long enough here to begin to be weary of a place where now almost every one is my junior, and therefore have resolved to retire to my living and fix for good and all there; and in order hereto I have hearkened to proposals that have been made to me of marriage, and because they are such as are very advantageous. I have already got so far as ye sealeing of articles, whereby I have secured to myself 3,000l; but after ye death of ye
ffather and mother, whose only child ye gentlewoman is, I believe there will be at least 1,500l more. I little thought I should ever come to this; but abundance of motives have overpowered me, and therefore I have yielded to the circumstances of my present condition, which would neither be convenient nor comfortable to me without this resolution. Although they are very few who I have yet communicated this to, I cannot conceal it from yourself. I doe not ask your advice herein, because it is too late for it; neither doe I your opinion, because you cannot judge of it without knoweing all my circumstances, which it would be too long for me now to tell you.
Norwich, October. 27th, 1686.

I am to beg your pardon that it hath been so long since I wrote to you. The truth is, I have been a long while in an unsettled condition, but now have fixed my self and all my concerns in this place, and shall be glad of a line or two to know of your health. Before I left Oxford I think I acquainted you how our accounts stand, and shall be answereable for what remains due unto you as you shall direct. Your brothers interest being so great at court I should think it might be made use of to get you an establishment in England, so that you might be no longer confined to a place where I fear all things may run into confusion. We live here remote from ye center of affairs and in a great deal of quiet; only fears from London sometimes alarm us here, but I still hope it may go much better with us then we think or doe deserve. Our Dean is here with us, and goes not to London because under his Majestys displeasure, but I hope that affair er long may be over. We have got here a very excellent person for our Bishop, which is a great comfort unto us. I shall be glad to know of your health and how affairs stand with you.
Norwich, July 12th 1688.

It hath been so long since I have heard from you that I begin to fear I must loose your correspondence. I confess we are now at a great distance; however I should be loath our old friendship should be forgot. Your brother being now a great man at Court, I have been expecteing that by his interest a translation might be procured for you to some place in the English Court as advantageous to you as that you have in ye Irish, and I hope some time or other it may be don, that I may have my good friend again where I may sometimes have ye happiness of enjoying his conversation. Things look cloudy upon us here, and ye matter of ye Declaration hath, I fear, put us much under the Kings displeasure. However, I thank God we still live in quiet, and, if God continues that, we may be content patiently to bear all things else. At present we are only hurt in imagination, and our greatest torment is our fears of what may after happen; but I hope they will prove to be only fears and nothing else. I hope when you come into England you may think Norwich worth your seeing, when you have a friend here that would so heartily make you welcome. I have now lived here 2 years in great content, it being ye most delightful city of any I have seen in England for a man to live in, especially in our distrinct, which hath all sorts of conveniences to recommend it to our satisfaction. There is still some money due unto you from me, and it hath lain in London for you now near these 2 years, but it being ye last account I am like to make with you I would gladly have your full discharge when it is paid you, and therefore I hope your occasions may er long call you to London, and then all things shall be made even between us. I confess I am ye more cautious because ye last 15l I paid you had like to have been lost through ye death of your kinsman to whom it was to be paid, and I only ow it to Mr Pitts negligence in omitteing to give him ye
bill when he ought that it was not. Pray favour me to let me hear from you when you have leisure, and you will very much oblige, etc.
Norwich , June 7th, 1691.

I should be glad to hear whether you have taken my advice in applying to Dr Sharpe in reference to your brother, and what success you have had in it. He is a generous, free spirited man, and would deal well with a chaplain, and in his station will be able to advance him. But as to ye other person you mentioned (whom I thoroughly know), all is ye contrary. He hath nothing in his gift fit for your brother to accept, and, if he had, he is a close designeing man that will reguard little but what tends to his own or relations interests, and I would by no means advise any friend of mine to list himself under him. Whatever ye Church may be advantaged by others of ye new promotion, I expect it will be very little by him. He is indeed my old friend and acquaintance; however, it grieves me to se this diocese sacrificed to his secular interest, he being one that will by no means answer its needs, and I think there is no diocese in England needs a good Bishop more then this. You see the London ministers get all ye preferments, and therefore, if possible, fix your brother there, and I assure you, as ye world now goes, a curacy is better then a living,
for, all country commodities being so low and taxes so high, all livings that depend upon prediall tiths are fallen more then half in value. I assure you ye living I now live at, although in common reputation 120l per annum, and so it was when I first took it, is not now worth 401 per annum clear of all charges, and therefore, till ye world be better, I would by no means advise you to putt your brother into such a living as would forfeit his fellowship, but reather to begin in some employment that might be consistent with it and make way for further provision; and in order to this I could not direct you better then to ye Archbishop of York, and I should be heartily glad to hear you have had any success with him.
Saham near Wanton, in Norfolk, October. 12th, 1691.

I doe most humbly thank you for ye favour of yours. I have been a while from home, otherwise you had been troubled from me er this. As to Dr Pococks place, it was offered me and I refused it, and that for two reasons: the first is, I nauseate that learning, and am resolved to loose no more time upon it; and the 2d is, I nauseate Christ Church; and, further, if I should go to Oxford again I must quit whatever I have here, and ye advantage would scarce pay for ye remove. But my main argument is, I have an unconquerable aversion to ye place, and will never live more among such people who now have ye prevaileing power there. I should be glad to be assured you are at the same lodgings, for I will send you a bill for ye remainder of your money in my hand, it being now in London for you. I am glad you have placed your brother as you mention; ye Earl of Pembroke hath good livings in his gift, and if they fall he can provide for him. Our Dean tells me that you have got now an employment; I should be glad to wish you joy of it, if I knew what. It seems you had him always with you at your coffee house, and I wish you had him there still for any good he doth at Norwich, for ye truth is, he is good for nothing
but his pipe and his pot, and we are wretchedly holpd up with him.
P.S. Sr Robert Baldoc that was judge in King James's reign is lately dead.
Norwich, June 13th, 1692.

I doe most heartily thank you for ye favour of yours, which were more then ordinarily welcome for ye sake of ye good news they brought. Till this happy turn our Jacobites were come to that height of confidence to talk openly that now all was their own, and some of them suspended their payment of ye taxes; and at ye bishops visitation at Norwich, which was the 3 latter days of Whitsun week, the Jacobite clergy would not own his jurisdiction and refused to appear; but on Sunday night ye news coming to us of ye victory, they came all the next day and made their submission, and I hope now they will have ye wit to carry themselves better, and if they doe not that ye government will have ye courage to call all such to an account. For in the strength of such a victory the King may now begin to act accordeing to his own measures. I remember, when last at London, I was with one of ye deprived Bishops, who seemed as confident of going again very speedily to his bishopric as I was of going home again, but I thank God he is like now to be disappointed. I perceive the French King and our Jacobites deceived each other; he made them believe wonders he would doe for them, and they made him believe as much that they would doe for him. I hope they will now be both undeceived, and an end be put to that great confidence which was between them. I have for 3 years been exceedeingly troubled at Ipswich
with an untoward clergyman there, one Alexander. He was lecturer of the town, a place very considerable, but, being turned out for his misdemeanour in ye beginneing of the revolution by the town on whom he depended, he got another church in ye town, although of little or no value, and there did nourish such a faction and division in ye place, and was so closely stuck to by ye Jacobites, as being looked on a martyr for that cause, that he had almost undone ye place in setteing the people together by ye ears. I had autority enough of my side to have routed him, and will enough to doe it, but found him backed by men of that power both in church and state that I durst not meddle with him for fear of draweing them upon myself, but reserved the case for ye Bp., his authority better enableing him to encounter him. But the truth is, I found his Lordship as cautious in the matter as myself, and the mischief must have gone on to ye utter undoing of this place, but that this Jacobite design, God be thanked, hath delivered us from him. It seems he, being an agent employed to give ye party warneing to be in readiness, put on a tinkers habit with a snapsack on his back, and so went on foot through all Essex; but in one place being discovered, where he had been too free of his talk as to ye design on foot, he was followed to Ipswich, and there seized on and laid in jail for treason, which putes an end to the whole controversy.
Saham near Wanton, in Norfolk, June 27th, 1692.

I have yours of the 16th, but it came not to my hands till last Friday, for I was absent at Ipswich on a visitation. I there had ye whole of Alexanders affair. He was lecturer of that place, but was turned out about 3 years since for several misdemeanours. To revenge himself for this, he hath lived in ye town ever since,
made a party there big enough to put the place into a flame ever since. At first I interposed with my autority to quench it, but finding him backed by the then Archbps. of Canterbury and York, whom he had made believe that he suffered for ye cause of the Church, I thought it best to let it alone, and so it hath stood ever since, and the town and he have been at law ever since; but on this advantage I suppose they will be too hard for him, for one of ye main reasons why he was turned out was his busy opposition to ye present Government, especially in one sermon which they say was ye cause of ye mutiny of ye Scotch soldiers that quartered there about 3 years since, which I suppose you may remember; and his present misdemeanour is a grand confirmation of that argument. The true story of his doings in Essex is, he came to Keldane in a gray coat and pair of bags on his back, which it seems by some was improved into a tinkers budgett, and lay there two days to wait for a coach to go for Ipswich. In the interim he makes it his endeavour to make his landlord a Jacobit; tells him King James was a coming; that if he would not declare for him him now he would be glad to doe it two months hence, for he was coming; that they were sure of ye major part of ye fleet; and a great deal more to this purpose; and that he had 3 horses ready to be employed in his service, whereof one was kept in London, and ye others elsewhere. However, it will be that advantage to ye town of Ipswich to get rid of him that, in case he will quit that place and create no more disturbances there, ye Bp. hath undertook to intercede for him; and I should be heartily glad ye cause would fall this way. He is a fellow of parts, but employs them mostly to doe mischief. The Bp. hath finished his visitation and is again gon to London, but it was little more then pro form` , for ye truth is, in our present case of unsettlement the times will not bear
doing more. The Act of Toleration hath almost undone us, not in increasing ye number of dissenters but of wicked and profane persons; for it is now difficult almost to get any to church, all pleadeing ye licence, although they make use of it only for ye alehouse. There must be a regulation in these matters, and yet it will be difficult to get a parliament sober enough to doe it. Phanaticisme hath got ye prevalence in corporations, and ye gentlemen must humour them this way or else they will not be chosen.
Norwich , Nov. 27th, 1693.

I have two of yours to thank you for, and I had not been so tardy in acknowledging the debt but that I tarried to have wherewith to make a return, which ye country is not so fertile of as ye city. Out of Suffolk I have full assurance that ye recorder of Oxford is sent thither of purpose to promote ye great design in hand. He is a stranger to that country, and on his first coming thither came with ye keepers letter and ye interest of ye Feltons to back it to make him recorder of that town. He calls himself a lawyer, and yet doth not practice; he seems to be a very fair conditioned good-tempered man, and thereby ye better capacitated to wheedle; but those that send me this character of him have not enabled me to tell you his name, but I have expressly wrote to be informed of it. I have been told also of a person of quality that hath made a tour this last summer through that whole country at ye gentlemen's houses for this purpose; so we see they turn every stone for their design, without considereing they serve none by it but the King of France; and indeed I have been lately told by a very intelligent person that he is well assured that abundance of those that seem fierce Republicarians are in reality fierce Jacobites, and that they openly promote this design for no other end but that it is ye likeliest to bring about what they would really have. Whenever there is a new parliament, the knights of ye shire for Norfolk will be Sr Henry Hobart and Sr Roger Pots, and for Suffolk Sr Samuel Bernardiston and Sr Jarvis Always, all stiff Republicarians; but I hope most of ye burroughs will provide better.
I am now at Norwich, where ye Dean behaves himself more like a beast then ever, and is so obstinate and perverse in his own humours (which are indeed intolerable) that there is no endureing of him. I find he is much in with the party, without considereing that if they prevail they will take his deanery from him; and indeed, if that were all the hurt they would doe, it would be no great matter. The Lt. Nottingham being now out, I suppose all that were put into employment by his means will follow ye same risk, which makes me concerned for you. I shall be glad to know what will be ye event in this matter. I confess, were I worthy to advise you, I should be desirous you still keep your place, although it be by temporiseing with them you cannot like. If ye Government stands, things must revert again to ye interest of those that now seem to be undermost, and my Lt. Nottingham will be in place again; for I look on it only as a trick to suit ye exigencies of ye times that ye King is forced to humour those men, and if once ye cause be removed ye effect of it will be so also.
Norwich , Dec. 11th, 1693 .

I have ye favour of yours, and by a letter from another friend ye names of all the pensioners. I am of opinion this discovery will so blast that party that we have no need to fear any thing from them this sessions. The Dialogue between Whig and Tory is with great eagerness dispersed here, and all that's said in it goes for gospel amongst too many. The poison is so taking that I think it needs an antidote. We are here at a miserable pass with this horrid sot we have got for our Dean. He cannot sleep at night till dosed with drink, and therefore, when in bed, his mans business is to drink with him till he hath his dose; and it being his way to keep a man only for ye time of his residence and then dismiss him, he hath spread his fame so through ye whole country that nothing is more scandalous; for his servants, whom he thus dismisses, going into other familys, tell all, especially one, a lewd fellow enough, being entertained by one Mr. Earl, a drinkeing lewd gentleman of this country, to be his butler, gives there a most horrid account of his old Mr ye Dean; and when ye lewd ones there meet together to drink, one of their chief entertainments is to have ye butler come in and tell all his stories of ye Dean of N., which represent him one of ye greatest beasts in nature. And indeed his carriage in business represents him as much a brute as his man can a beast, for he acts by no rules of justice, honesty, civility, or good manners towards any one, but after an obstinate, selfe-wild, irrational manner in all sorts of businesses, whereby he disoblidgeth every one that hath
any thing to doe with him. He hath after a most unreasonable manner disoblidged every one of the prebendarys except Hodges, and nothing will satisfy him but to be an absolute king over us. He comes little to church and never to ye sacrament, though we have a sacrament every Sunday; and as for a book, he looks not into any from ye beginning of ye year to ye end. His whole life is ye pot and ye pipe, and, go to him when you will, you will find him walking about his room with a pipe in his mouth and a bottle of claret and a bottle of old strong beer (which in this country they call nog) upon ye table, and every other turn he takes a glass of one or ye other of them. If Hodges comes to him (for scarce any other doth), then he reads Don Quixote, while ye other walks about with his pipe as before, and this is noble entertainment between them. Certainly ye preferments of ye Church were never designed for such drones; and yet these two fellows have about 300l per annum each, and never did it a farthings worth of service in their life, professeing nothing else but to live idly and feed their bellies upon what they have. Hodges indeed is no drinker as ye other, for his body cannot bear it; but although nothing is more mean then he, either in his birth or his merit, yet nothing can be more proud and conceited, or possibly can have a more despicable thought then he hath of the business of his profession, and, to tell ye truth, he is not made for it. Once in a year he will offer to preach, but, his sermons being most on end ye translation of his moral philosophy lectures at Oxford, as soon as ye people see him in ye pulpit they all get out of church. Nothing could be more humble and complaisant then this fellow was all the time of ye 2 late Kings, when he was obnoxious on ye account of his Mr, Shaftsbury, or can there be any thing more proud and insolent then he hath appeared ever since this government began. But I hope after all their point will not go. This discovery of
pensioners I reckon will break ye reputation of ye party, especially if it be pursued with 2 or 3 pamphlets, which I heartily wish for. The late Archbp. would be buried in ye churchyard and by a Nonjuror. Dr Trumball, his quondam chaplain, performed that office for him. His library he gave to Emmanuel College in Cambridge, whither he sent it before his death. The reason of his being buried in the churchyard, I am told, was no other but to lie among his relations who are buried there. A friend of mine wrote me from London yt ye Earl of Nottingham may be Secretary again if he will, and ye Earl of Shrewsbury's refusal having put ye King out of all his measures and much exasperated him against that party who assured him yt Earl would accept of ye place, several of our members went out of this country prepared to fall upon the church this sessions; but now, I hope, we shall escape their malice this bout. Our Bp. will never accept of Dublin; he acts here as wise and cunning a part as possibly a man can doe, and will make his fortune any where, and therefore you may be assured he will never leave England. I find the Republicarians in these parts openly sedulous to promote atheism, to which end they spread themselves in coffy houses and talk violently for it, and Dr Burnets Archaiologia is much made use of by them to confute ye account ye Scriptures give us of ye creation of ye
world, and other books are also dispersed for this purpose, and ye number of their proselytes I am assured is great. You see where licentiousness and confusion at last end.
Norwich , April 15, 1696.

The account which is given in one of ye prints, called ye "Post boy," of the Association of this place gives ye governors of this city great disgust; ffor ye truth is, every word of it is false, and it foully reflects upon them. Ye whole spring of that contrivance I told you in my last, and indeed, considereing ye notion which those had of the word "revenge" who were so zealous for it, there was good reason for ye altereing of it. For they declared they meant thereby that, in case ye King was kilt,they would draw their swords and cut ye throats of all ye Jacobites, and that by virtue of the Parliaments Association they were bound thereto; which extravagance deserved to be discountenanced and disowned; for should ever ye case happen, which God forbid, every man shall be a Jacobite whom ye rabble shall think fit to plunder and abuse. Next Friday our seven condemned criminals are to be executed. They are stout fellows all of them, but as hardened villains as ever I heard of in my life. All that those ministers who assist them can doe to make them sensible of their condition avails nothing, and those few minutes they have left they spend in the height of lewdness and frolic. The Mayor hath ordered ye town clerk of ye city now in
London to prosecute ye writer of ye "Post boy" for slandering them in his print, unless he will discover the intelligencer that sent him ye news from hence, and then they will right themselves of him here on the place. The truth is, whoever wrote that account to him was a very impudent lying fellow, and by one passage I perceive intends a reflection on me, as if I influenced the city to ye alteration; whereas nothing is a more constant rule with me then never to meddle with any of their concerns, and indeed I very seldom go among them. Our close is as it were a town of itself apart from ye city, separated from it by walls and gates. I acknowledge I have as great a share of their respects as any of my profession perchance that hath ever lived among them, but I take care to have nothing at any time to doe with them but in my profession, and in this they have my pains constantly gratis. I am afraid we shall have but a lame return from ye clergy to whom we have sent our Association to be subscribed; it is a very moderate form, and I have sent this argument with it into my archdeaconry: that the ready subscribeing of it will be ye surest way to prevent an harder form from being imposed on us. I have taken all ye care I can to induce all, where I am concerned, to comply. I need not trouble you with a copy of ye form; I suppose you have it at London.
Norwich, April 17th, 1696.

This day ye sentence was executed upon those desperate villains who were condemned at ye last assizes; and their last effort had something in it more then ordinary. Those that brought them their coffins conveyed to them therein arms, provisions, and other things, in order to an escape; which having got, they knocked of their irons and made an attempt to break out, but, not being able to succeed, they took possession of ye dungeon, into which there was only one narrow passage, and there stood several days
upon their guard. But this morneing, by help of ye soldiers that quarter here, they forced ye place and took ye malefactors, whereon one of them immediately took poison, to prevent ye execution, but by poring oil into his mouth they made him cast it up again, so he lived long enough to be hanged with the rest. They were seven desperate sturdy villains, and we are well rid of them. When they came to ye gallows they did lament that they had been deceived by some at London, who fed them with promises of pardon, and so dyed in a manner by surprise without making any use of ye time which they had between sentence and execution. Yesterday ye Thanksgiveing day was kept here in a more then ordinary manner, the Mayor being willeing to doe more then ordinary to relieve himself from ye slur cast upon him about ye Association by ye weavers and their correspondent, ye writer of ye "Post boy." Next May day they choose a new Mayor; ye man next in order, and who will certainly be chosen, is one Mr Bikerdike, who is ye most intelligent person of ye whole body.
Norwich , April 24th, 1696.

There is this morneing gon from hence towards London one Dr Bambridge, a physician of this place. His business is to solicit Mr Tasboroughs discharge, in order to which he is to apply to ye Duke of Norfolk , with whom he is very dear whenever his Grace comes hither. I have many years looked on him as a very dangerous person. His practice cannot be worth him 40l per annum, and yet he lives at ye rate of 400l per annum, without any visible estate. Everybody looks on him here as a great mystery. Most will have it that he lives by ye trade of a stallion; but no one can tell where he should have trade enough this way to maintain him as he lives. For my part I have looked on him for
those ten years to have been a spy for ye papists. I am sure he acted for their interest strenuously in ye late reign, and is continually with them now, and is their servant on all occasions. But as to religion, he hath none but that which will best serve his interest. Some one put in an information against him to the Council table since this plot broke out, but ye Duke of Norfolk got him of. One part of his instructions are, I hear, to know, what informations are against Mr Tasborough, and from whom. If Mr Tasborough be discharged, I wish it may be on condition that he leave this place, where he hath don a great deal of mischief. His business here is looked on to be to manage the correspondence of ye party in receiving and sendeing all letters, for which they have messengers of their own. Two of them were observed to have been here on ye breaking out of ye plot, and, as soon as they had ye news of it, immediately took horse and rod away. Sr Robert Yallup, Sr Christopher Calthrop, and Sr Nicholas Lestrange, yesterday, upon summons, appeared at the sessions and had ye oaths tendered to them; but all refused. Ye latter paid his 5l and found security accordeing to law, but ye other two refused both, and so are committed. Sr Robert Yallup is ye greatest knave in nature, but ye other two very honest gentlemen. Sr Nicholas Lestrange is a man of parts, virtue, and prudence, but cannot at present conform to ye taking of ye oaths; but Sr Christopher Calthrop a man of strong zeal and weak judgement and totally bigoted to Torisme, but one whom I reckon a harmless man and no otherwise inclined to show his affection to ye cause he is in but by suffering for it; and he seems in his present acteings to court suffereing. I am of opinion that ye Government, as to him, would best serve its interest by dischargeing him.
Norwich, June 1,1696.

I am now returned again from my Suffolk journey, where I found all things very quiet. Ye long struggle which hath been between the two parties in yt country is now totally at an end by ye absolute victory which ye Whig party hath got over ye other. For they have not only carried all ye elections from them in ye last Parliament, but have also made them criminals for opposing them, having brought indictments of riot against them at ye last assizes on this account, and by a packd jury (5 of which were ye members chosen, who came down from the Parliament of purpose for this job) caused ye bills to be found against them, which hath sent ye other party to London with a petition for a noli prosequi ; but those persons who were thus used (and some of them are ye worthiest gentlemen of ye country) are exceedeingly soured against ye Government on this account, which by no means tends
to ye Kings interest, or doe I find any one pleased with it but Sr Robert Rich and his gang. Our mayor is like again to recover since sequesterd from ye brandy bottle. I find ye difficulties about ye coin to press hard everywhere all ye way I came, but I hope the mint will take care speedily to remedy this inconvenience.
Norwich , July 20th, 1696.

I am sorry ye matter of Sr C. C. did raise such a storm; but some men delight in mischief, and such seldom fail at last of having enough of it upon their own heads. Here hath been of late sculkeing in this town the Archbp. of Glasco, to whom ye Jacobites of the place did much resort. I wish here be not more mischief a breweing, for that party begins again to be very confident and insolent. The Archbp. is now at Yarmouth and there much caressed as I hear. Sr John Barker, one of ye burgesses of Ipswich, lys in a very languishing condition, not like to recover. His death, I believe, will reconcile the town and bring them all again to be of a piece, which hath been in perpetual feuds for these seven or 8 years last past. I intend, if I can, to persuade my Lt Huntingtowr to stand there in case of a vacancy, who is a very sensible man, and with great prudence manageth all affairs that he putts his hands unto, only, having come to an incumberd estate, that frugality and spareing way of living which his circumstances at first made necessary hath habituated him to that which,now he is out of those circumstances, is downright stinginess. For he, having now cleared his estate of ye vast debt which he found
upon it, may very well afford to live accordeing to his quality. After his mother ye Duchess of Lauderdale, and his mother-in-law ye Lady Wilbraham, he will have better then 3000l per annum. For Sr Thomas Wilbraham had only two daughters to inherit his estate, which was large. Mr Newport married one, and ye Lt Huntingtowr ye other. He lives most on end near Harborough in Northamptonshire; but ye principal seat of his family is at Helmingham, 7 miles from Ipswich. Here hath lately been in this place one that calls himself Archbishop of Glascoe. The papists did not appear at ye sessions; they say they will return them convict at ye next assizes. I should be glad could I see it, for then ye University would have the disposal of their livings, which now they give to ye worst men they can find. The difficulties about money still grow more presseing. Mr Hodges being here hath received an invitation from Mr Lock, to desire a visit from him, in terms that bespeaks him a dying man.
Norwich , Aug. 24, 1696 .

We have had here a long assizes, it having continued from Saturday last was seven-night till this evening. On ye Crown side there have been two condemned for murder and one for clippeing and coineing. Att ye other bar ye most remarkable cause hath been between two clergymen, Dean and Williams; ye later about 3 years since married a widow whom we reckoned worth 1500l; ye other pretends a contract and sues Williams upon it, and this time twelmonth had a verdict and 200l damage. Hereon Williams
pleads Dean to be guilty of forgery in forgoing ye said contract and several other love letters produced to prove that contract, and upon a long trial of 9 hours last assizes Dean was found guilty of ye forgery; but he having obtained another trial, it was this assizes tried over again, and it took up a whole days hearing, and ye jury were locked up a whole night, and at last, through ye obstinacy of one man, the forgerer was acquitted, though his guilt manifestly appeared to every stander-by at ye trial, and ye Judge yesterday at dinner, when I dined with him, fully expressed himself as to Deans guilt; and indeed he is as ill a man as any of his profession in the countey, and the other as honest a man. This affair hath made much noise and is not yet at an end; there will be another trial about it. Sr Christopher Calthorps affair is much talked of. Sr Roger Pots, one concerned against him, would have persuaded a gentleman to have wrote to Sr C. C. to render himself prisoner again at ye assizes, for, said he, this may prevent a great deal of trouble in Parliament; for it seems Sr Henry Hobart threatens he will bring this matter into Parliament. However ye Lord Chief Justice Treby at this assizes hath judged in effect his commitment to be illegal, as really it was; ffor he was committed for not finding security on his second refusal of ye oaths, whereas the first was before ye act of pardon and pardond by it, and, if pardond by it, it cannot certainly operate to make a second offence; for, in that it is pardond, it must fall under oblivion and not be any more remembered, and therefore certainly must not be brought into any reckoneing in order to make a second offence; and when this was pleaded this assizes, in behalf of Sr Nicholas Lestrange who had given security in the same case, that he was illegally put upon it because ye first offence was pardoned, the judge allowed the plea and discharged him. However, ye Duke of Norfolk, who is
now here, talks that there will be an order of Council again to recommitt Sr C. C.; and if such a thing should be moved, I wish it might be granted, and let those men who trouble themselves so much in this affair take ye shame of it; ffor ye illegality of his commitment will be manifested, whenever an opportunity shall be given for it. The D. of N. brought down one Mrs Lane. his mis, with him, who made a great show here; however he failed of his main purpose, which was to entertain himself with ye ladies; for, when he had made great preparations for a ball, none would come to it, which gave him yt offence that he said he would never make one here more; and I think it is time for him to leave it of, when all that have any reguard to their reputations think it scandalous to accept his invitations. Our mint doth not yet work, and ye difficulties about ye coin grow worse and worse. Sr John Barker dyed Friday last was seven-night. It is not yet known, or as far as I can hear as much as conjectured, who will stand for the place.
Norwich , May 28, 1697.

Dr Smith, one of our prebendarys, dyed last Tuesday. He was a very vigorous old man, and, although past 80, had the strength of
a man of 40; but, being taken with an inflammation of ye bladder, ye surgeon who searched him gave his judgement positively that he had a very great stone in his bladder, which misguideing his physicians, they gave him over as desperate; but when opend after his death the mistake appeared, and, had it not been for this mistake, he might easily have been cured and lived many years more. I am now come to be ye senior of our church save one, it being ye 17th year that I have been here prebendary. All this country continues very quiet, and money is now as plentiful among us as ever, and trade begins to grow as brisk. My bookseller writes me that he hath already sold of one impression of my book and is now on a second edition. I have by me a system of the Mohammedan divinity, which is ye oddest stuff that I believe you ever saw; but to ad this will double ye bulk of ye book, which will not be for ye booksellers profit now paper is so dear. This would make that book complete. Perchance paper may be cheaper by that time ye 2d edition is of, and then it shall be ready to be inserted into ye 3d. The life of Mahomet I find is a novelty that makes ye book acceptable. The expectation of a peace is in every bodies mouth, and all very greedily run after ye news to se how it proceeds; and indeed ye taxes are now sufficiently heavy to make them weary of ye war.
Norwich , June 4th, 1697.

All this country is filled with very melancholy stories in reference to our present circumstances. They represent Jamaica lost, Aeth taken, the King and ye Duke of Bavaria parted in a feud never to be reconciled again, and that King William is deserted by all ye confederates and left to shift for himself, it
being certainly agreed by them to make a peace without him; that, unless ye House of Austria doth consent to such a peace, the French are strong enough immediately to possess themselves of all Flanders and Catalonia; and that we are to be sacrificed to prevent it. If this be our case, it is bad enough with a vengeance. I should be very sorry to see cause to believe any of it; but, were our circumstances well, I scarce think men would be thus bold with ye Government in representeing its case in such a manner. However, as far as it is false, I would be glad to have it authentically refuted. Nothing else from hence worth your knowledge.
Norwich , June 14, 1697.

I thank you for ye favour of yours. The Jacobites here grow higher than ever; but an accident happened last Thursday which I believe will cut their combs a little. It being the Prince of Wales's birthday, about 16 of them met at a tavern to drink his health, and among others there was one Captain Ogilby, who had formerly been a captain in Dumbartons Regiment, and hath some years skulked here with a certain widow woman of this country that kept him to serve her purposes. He, with one Doedale and Riley, two Irish papists, and one Caps, a papist of this town, were ye last that left ye bottle. At 12 they broke up and went all 4 home together; on ye way, Doedale and Ogilby quarrelleing, ye later was run thorough and is since dead. Doedale is fled, but ye other two are still on ye place, and I think in law must answer for ye fact, for they are proved all 4 to have had their swords drawn, and ye other two fled ye streets as soon as Ogilby fell. I am told an ejectment hath been left at Sr H. Hobarts house for 8000l, which will reach a great part of his estate. I have been informed out
of Suffolk that ye dissenters there are busy upon some designs relating to their interest, against ye next Parliament. I have sent to have it sifted into, and, if there be any thing in it, you shall have an account of it. One of our aldermen, a very rude huffeing fellow, was on Saturday condemned by ye Court of Aldermen to ye stool of repentance for abuseing one of his brethren, that is, to beg his pardon publicly before ye Court in a form prescribed him, and subscribe his hand to it in their public register to stand upon record; and next Wednesday is assigned him for ye day, on penalty of being expelled out of his aldermans place. He is a proud insolent fellow and rich, so the city is in expectation what he will doe. If he refuses it, as by his temper I suspect he will, there will be work for ye lawyers.
Norwich , Sept. 30, 1698.

I am now returned from my Suffolk journey. While I was there ye Earl of Orford came to Orford to influence ye election of a mayor there, and was expected at Beccles this week at Sr Robert Riches, who was making preparations for his reception when I was there last Monday. Sr Robert came to my inn to visit me, and overpowered me with his civilities, and of these I find he is very liberal to other people in his good moods; but, when his passion takes its turn, he vents that in so unreasonable a manner, even upon ye same persons, that I find he hath scarce any interest but among ye dissenters, who in that corner have no other support but what they have from him. There is one Le Pell, an officer in the Danish auxiliary that came over here, who hath caught a young heiresse in my archdeaconry worth 15000l, and he not worth 5 groats. Ye young woman indeed was no beauty, but was reckoned to have wit and discretion; but she miserably betrayed ye want of the latter in this particular. Her name was Brookes. Mr Whitacre, Recorder of Ipswich, who served for that place last Parliament, I find hath so far lost himself in that corporation that he will scarce ever recover himself there again. The Lt.
Paston is like to be chosen at Thetford in ye place of Sr Joseph Williamson, who hath let that corporation know that he intends to serve for Rochester. His letters to that corporation in ye behalf of Sloane were in a more than ordinary strain in his favour, calleing him in every line his dear Sloane, and telleing them that they could not be kind to him if they were not so to his dear Sloane also. However, that corporation gets but little credit by this choice. The Duchess of Grafton hath been with her son, ye young Duke, at Euston Hall ever since July; but this next week she goes for London.
Norwich , May 9, 1705.

The Norwich cause is now going up to the Council, the ffreemen having delivered a petition to ye Lord Townshend, to be presented to ye Queen and Council, against the Mayor and
Aldermen, for depriving them of their rights; and the Lord Townshend hath undertaken that it shall be delivered. The case is thus. One Mr Briggs, an alderman, dying ye 3rd of August last, there appeared candidates in that ward for his place Mr Dunch and Mr Austin. Mr Dunch being a sturdy Whig and a fellow of notable parts and understandeing, the Mayor, who is a sturdy Tory, resolved to doe all he could to keep him out; and therefore, although the elections in such cases used to be made within 10 or 12 days, the Mayor deferred it till ye middle of ye last month, hoping in all this time to make sure of a party to keep Dunch out; but it hapneing to work ye contrary way, Dunches party grew by ye delay, and he was chosen by a great majority. Whereon ye Mayor and his party in the Court of Aldermen claimed a right of approveing the alderman chosen, and they would not approve the election of Dunch, but rejected him, giving him for their reasons of so doing that he was a turbulent, malicious man, and of uncivil behaviour in conversation; and ordered ye ward to choose again. The ward met and chose Dunch again, but, notwithstandeing, the Mayor hath sworn in Austin, taking, I suppose, all ye votes given for Dunch to go for nothing. Hereon Dunch hath served mandamus upon the Mayor out of the Kings Bench, and there ye point now is. I find none of their charters can justify their claim to an approbation. They have an instance in their books of an alderman once chosen by ye ward and disapproved by ye Court of Aldermen; but all their charters seem to be quite ye contrary, that ye Mayor is to swear in whomsoever the ward chooses. This is like to creat a great ruffle here, and I take it Blofield will certainly be flung out for being of the Mayors party in this matter. I was apprehensive of it some time since,and took notice to Blofield of it; but his over-confidence in his party made him neglect ye advice I gave him.
Norwich, June 25th, 1705.

A rumour hath been here for some time that you have of late been under some trouble; although ye experience which now I have had for near 40 years of your untainted integrity doth give me full assurance that nothing of that which is said can stick upon you, yet to be assured from yourself that all is made clear will be a great satisfaction to me. I beg this favour of you.
Norwich, July 11, 1705.

I am very sorry you have suffered that trouble and damage which you mention. Whatsoever may have brought this misfortune upon you I can never think otherwise of you than I have always known and experienced for so many years, and I hope you will so clear this matter as to maintain your reputation as fully and as entirely with every body else as you always must with me; for, whatever becomes of your place, I would advise you by no means to give up ye reputation of your integrity, but vindicate that to ye utmost you are able, that, although you are not in ye same post you were, yet still you may be looked on as ye same honest man. There being few I have had more friendship from than from yourself, I cannot but be very much grieved at this misfortune which hath happened to you, and I assure you I bear my share with you in it.
Norwich, Nov. 26, 1707.

I acquainted you in my last with ye case of ye Yarmouth petition, which I am much concerned to oppose; because it lays a great encumbrance upon my estate. To hinder its progress, I have drawn the enclosed petition to be subscribed by myself and others who will be damaged by it; but, being ignorant of the stile and usual form in which such petitions are addressed to ye House, the favour which I beg of you is, that you would put it into due form where it is defective, and put the stile of address so as it ought to be, and then send it me back again, that I may get it wrote out fair and subscribed, that so it may be lodged ready to be presented, if their shall be an occasion. But I am of opinion that, when it becomes known that a counter petition is ready, the petition will never be at all presented; for I think it cannot stand against the reasons which we offer against it. I humbly beg your pardon for this trouble which I give you.
Norwich, March 31, 17078 .

I doe very much thank you for ye favour of yours, and am glad that the Scotch plot is over. I reckon ye Court plot for confoundeing the Ministry and the City plot for the breaking of the Bank and ye East Inti Company are all branches of it, which argues it to be a very deep laid design, and I doubt we doe not yet see half way into the bottom of it. I wish it doe not hereafter break out in some other mischief. I am of opinion people will be willing enough to overlook ye Queens mistake in the matter of the Ministry, provided the Admiralty be better provided
for; but ye generality are so exceedeingly dissatisfied with ye present management of that, that they will never cease clamoureing till that great trust be in other hands. And, indeed, I wonder at the indiscretion of those counsels which influence the continueing of the Prince in such a post, where he is only to bear ye blame of other men's miscarriages. Had the Bank broke when ye run was made upon it, I must have broke too, for I had then 4000l in it; but I have now disposed of it to ye purpose for which it lay there. I hope I shall never again have the occasion of running such an hazard. I reckon ye matters that have been of late transacted will, on this baffle, have a great influence on this next election. I wish it doe not carry the Whig interest too high, for that is best when well balanced. I durst not trust them when paramount; whenever they are so, I am afraid they will be making dangerous attempts. I pray God all things may go well at last; at present I think we are much unjointed.
Norwich, Sept. 13,1708.

All that I can tell you from hence is, that now taxes begin to come very heavy; and the reason is, that rent comes heavier from the tenants; and, when ye land lord receives nothing, how can he pay anything? The failure of the countryman's trade is ye cause of this. We are now upon a very tickelish point abroad. If this campaign doth not succeed so well as to force the French to a peace next winter, I am afraid we shall not be able to find ffunds for another year. The event shows our victory at Oudenard
was no great matter, and we are not strong enough to have any prospect of gaining another, and without gaining another I doubt ye campaign may end to our disadvantage. Our new bishop is gon again to London; he hath set himself in here in a very good interest in his diocese, being generally as much in every mans good opinion as his predecessor was in the contrary. He hath been at great expense about his house, which, from a very ugly one, he hath made very convenient and handsome; but it is likely to cost him several hundred of pounds before he hath don. The Earl of Yarmouth is as low as you can imagine; he hath vast debts, and suffers every thing to run to extremity; so his goods have been all seized in execution and his lands extended, so that he hath scarce a servant to attend him or an horse to ride abroad upon, and yett cannot be persuaded to take any method of putteing his affairs into a better posture, which they are still capable of, if he would set about it. But ye Lord Townshend flourished much among us, for ye whole countey is absolutely at his beck, and he hath got such an ascendant here over everybody by his courteous carriage that he may doe anything among us what he will, and that not only in the countey, but also in all the corporations, except at Thetford, where all is sold. Ye election there is among the magistracy, and 50 guineas for a vote is their price. One Mr Boils, a stranger, was their last chapman, to whom they say they have sold themselves much dearer; for it hath cost him 3000l to get a return from thence for the next Parliament, and that is but a litigious one, for Sr John Woodhouse will be a petitioner against him.
Norwich, July 11, 1709.

I thank you for your kindness to my nephew. He did not let me know of this intended ramble till he was ready to be gon, and therefore it was too late for me to dissuade him from it. I know not what advantage it can bring him, and I am afraid it may doe him a great deal of hurt. My opinion hath been that it would be best for him to marry and settle at home upon his estate, which is better than 1000l per annum; but ye young man hath an ambition to make himself somewhat greater than a country gentleman, and, to give him his due, he hath a capacity for any thing, had he had an education suitable to it; and this it is he hopes to mend by travelling. I hope the new commotions in France may make it necessary for that Crown forthwith to make peace upon the preliminaries agreed, and thereby prevent the fatigues, which otherwise our army must be harassed with, in carrying on a siege in a wet season. My Lord of Norwich is now thoroughly recovered and gon into Suffolk to complete his visitation. Mr Clerk is now here and speaks gratefully to me of your respects to him. He is a person of great learneing and integrity, and I hope he will answer in all things else. His greatest preferment, in being made Rector of your parish, is in that hereby he is emancipated from the Bishop of Ely, whose service and ways he was heartily weary of. That man hath lately made one Dr Canon a Prebendary of his church, on contract to marry his daughter; and it is hard to say which is the greatest fool of the two in this matter. Canon is about 50 years and a very infirm man, being exceedingly troubled with ye
falleing of ye gut, which usually takes him up all the morneing to get it up; and she is a young sanguine girl of about 24. That he should at all marry in such a case and such an one as will be sure to loath him, or that ye other should marry such a daughter to such a man, is a folly on both sides which is not to be accounted for, and must end ill on both sides. I reckon the wedding is about this time. Canon is a favourite of ye Lord Treasurer, as having been tutor to his son at Cambridge, and, to give him his due, is a man of worth and learneing; and I suppose his father-in-law expects, on this bottom, to raise him in the Church, perchance to a bishopric. He is already Archdeacon of Norfolk, Prebendary of Ely, and Chaplain to Chelsey Hospital. I hear Dr Robinson is sent for over to be Bishop of Chichester, and I hope he will be a very fit man for it; and his interest with the northern protestants may be of great use to unite them with the Church of England. Should ye present Archbp. hold out a year longer, perchance by that time he may be thought of as a fit person to succeed him; and, if he should hold out so long, I would hope by that time ye man now talked of may be so truly represented to ye Queen as not to be approved of by her for that station; and I hear there are many at work to convince her of it, and that she is daily told something or other by those about her to this purpose. The Professor of Divinity at Oxford hath lately married a wife out of this country, and it is a very scandalous match; however, he became drawn into it. She is the daughter of one Coll. Venner, son to the famous Venner that was ye head of the Fifth Monarchy
men. This man served ye Venetians in the Morea, and was there a Coll. He, being in Holland when K. William came over, engaged with him in that expedition, and had a regiment in Ireland, and was entrusted with ye government of the hospital of ye army; but, being for his falseness in the management of that trust broken and discarded, he hath retired into this country and hath lived here several years, but with ye worst reputation that you can imagine in all respects, and is one of the most ill-looked fellows that ever I saw in my life, for he had occasion once to appear before me when on public business, and this was ye only time I ever saw him. But you cannot be a stranger to this mans character, and such an alliance cannot be to the credit of ye Professor; and they tell me it is as bad on ye mothers side as on ye fathers, who is daughter to one Dr Gardiner (as they call him), one that practises physic in Covent Garden. The Christ Church men, I apprehend, will make work with him upon this marriage.
Norwich, Dec. 26, 1709.

I thank you for ye favour of yours and the trouble which you are pleased, on my request, to take on you of disposeing of ye two books I sent you. I beg your pardon that I thus presume on you; your many favours in other matters have encouraged me also in this to rely upon you. I am glad what I have in this book published gives you satisfaction. I doe not expect so to come of with others, because I go not ye usual way in driveing this matter to those heights where it cannot stand, though I hear the Archbp. likes it well. Another part was intended when I begun, which would
